sweep_summary: Ket (kett1243) is in the catalog as classification lexical, deciding source Georg 2007:58-60 (held PDF). this search of works with stress in the title's two title hits are both first-hand, on-topic, and unread: Vajda 2000 'Ket Prosodic Phonology' (Lincom, 22 pp.) has no open copy anywhere reached (no HathiTrust item, Google Books no preview, Georg's 2002 Language book notice paywalled at DOI 10.1353/lan.2002.0156, Vajda's WWU site gone and the Internet Archive offline), and Werner 1996 'Vergleichende Akzentologie der Jenissej-Sprachen' (Harrassowitz, viii+168 pp.) is HathiTrust search-only (mdp.39015041372171) and Harvard offsite print. Second-hand evidence from held sources fixes what they contain: Georg 2007 cites Vajda 2000:2 (monosyllabic tone diagrams) and :20 (phonological-word boundaries) and, at p.60 fn.70, says 'Much of the following [the polysyllabic accent account] is based on' Werner 1996's experimental data (diagrams from Werner 1996:58:60; exceptions at :66ff.); Nefedov 2015 cites Vajda 2000:4-8 and Werner 1996:66ff. Both items therefore get priority high, Werner 1996 first, as the empirical base of the catalog's deciding statement. Re-reading Georg 2007 p.58/p.60 confirms the catalog's classification (two contours on the first two syllables of the phonological word, fifth/initial as default, sixth/second-syllable lexically and morphologically restricted); nothing read contradicts it. Crossref, Glottolog, Open Library, archive.org search and the HathiTrust catalog API were used instead.

new_statements.quote: p.60: 'The prosodic behaviour of tri-, quadrisyllabic and longer morpheme chains is more complicated and has not been subject to intense scrutiny[70]. Only few fairly recurrent patterns can be mentioned here, possibly only tendencies. The default rule is that the first two syllables of the phonological word receive one of the two disyllabic contours described above, leaving any syllable further to the right as a toneless appendix; most common is the fifth contour' — fn.70: 'However, Werner 1996 must be mentioned, where a great number of empirical data has been assembled. Much of the following is based on this source and its examples'.

new_statements.reading: This is the catalog's existing deciding source, re-read at page level in this search of works with stress in the title (no first-hand text of either works with stress in the title was obtainable). It states that a Ket phonological word of two or more syllables carries one of two pitch contours on its first two syllables: the 'fifth' contour (rise on syllable 1, fall on syllable 2; 'acoustic impression.. of a dynamic accent on the first syllable', p.57), which is the default and most common, versus the rarer 'sixth' contour (peak on syllable 2), whose choice is 'largely unpredictable' and lexically/morphologically tied (compounds, some plurals; minimal pairs ásel 'snowshoe' : àsel 'ilimka-boat', qóqbun 'cuckoo' : qòqbun 'cuckoos', p.58). That confirms the catalog's classification lexical with the {10…0, 010…0} rule set and an initial dominant pattern. The new information from this search of works with stress in the title is provenance: Georg explicitly bases his polysyllabic account on Werner 1996's instrumental data (fn.70; diagrams from Werner 1996:58 and :60), so Werner 1996 — a works with stress in the title — is the primary empirical source behind the deciding source and is the top acquisition target, ahead of Vajda 2000.

new_statements.quote: Zu den wichtigsten typologischen Besonderheiten der ketischen Phonologic gehort zweifellos die Silbentonalitat, die in den 60er Jahren gleich nach der jugischen (Vemer 1966; 1968) entdeckt und beschrieben wurde [p.20] ... Man kann im Ketischen zwei Tonsysteme unterscheiden - das siid- und nordketische - , die sich voneinander nach dem Charakteristikum des vierten Tones und zum Teil nach der lexikalischen Distribution der Tone unterscheiden. [p.21] ... AuBerdem kommt hier der vierte Ton in der crsten Silbe zweisDbiger Worter vor, denn diese Worter kennen keine Apokope des Endvokals, wie es der Fall im siidketischen Dialekt ist [p.22]
new_statements.translation: Among the most important typological peculiarities of Ket phonology is without doubt syllable tonality, which was discovered and described in the 1960s right after that of Yugh (Werner 1966; 1968) [p.20] ... In Ket one can distinguish two tone systems - South Ket and North Ket - which differ from one another in the character of the fourth tone and partly in the lexical distribution of the tones. [p.21] ... Moreover, here [in the Central and North Ket dialects] the fourth tone occurs in the first syllable of disyllabic words, because these words have no apocope of the final vowel, as is the case in the South Ket dialect [p.22]
new_statements.citation: Werner, Heinrich. 1997. Die ketische Sprache. (Tunguso-Sibirica 3.) Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, viii+405 pp. — section 2.4 'Akzentuation' beyond p.23 (word accent in polysyllables).
new_statements.locator: Sec. 2.4 Akzentuation, 2.4.1 Die Silbentonalität, printed pp.20-22 (Rosetta excerpt rosettaproject_ket_phon-3 = printed pp.11-23; lines 1305-1402); minimal quadruplet p.22; tone feature tables 5-6 p.23. The contents page (contents-2 excerpt, p.V) lists 2.4 Akzentuation as pp.20-25, so the part after p.23 (word accent in polysyllables) is outside the open copy.
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with and underlying the catalog's existing Georg 2007 statement (Georg's two disyllabic pitch contours are built on Werner's syllable tones; Georg fn.70 cites Werner 1996). It adds the four-tone inventory of monosyllables, the South/North Ket tone-system split and the fact that in Central/North Ket disyllables the 4th tone is on the first syllable, which is consistent with the initial-dominant pattern. It gives no placement rule for word stress in polysyllables (that part of 2.4 lies beyond p.23, outside the open excerpt), so it neither confirms nor contradicts the catalog's initial rule string; p.21 and fn.14 refer the reader to Werner 1996: 22-36 for the fuller treatment.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the open pages Werner treats Ket 'accentuation' as syllable tonality: every monosyllable carries one of four phonologically distinctive tones (1 half-long, evenly rising, ~30% of monosyllables; 2 short, glottalized/pharyngalized rise-fall, ~40%; 3 long, smooth rise-fall, ~20%; 4 short falling in South Ket, ~10%, but long low-register rise-fall in Central/North Ket), proved by the quadruplet s'ul' 'blood' / 'whitefish' / 'polar sledge' / 'cradle hook' (p.22). Tone system differs by dialect (South vs North Ket). In Central/North Ket the 4th tone sits on the first syllable of disyllables that keep their final vowel (sket. as' ~ nket. a:s'e 'feather'). No rule for the placement of word stress in polysyllables appears in the open pages; that subsection of 2.4 (after p.23) is not in the excerpt.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the open pages.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect differences: the fourth tone is short and falling in South Ket but long, low-register rise-fall in Central and North Ket; Central Ket (Surgutikha) often shortens 4th-tone syllables (fn.15); tone shape and length depend on syllable type (open / obstruent-closed / sonorant-closed; points 1-4 pp.22-23, fn.16); some speakers add a vocalic echo after the glottal stop in 2nd-tone open syllables (fn.13); 3rd-tone syllables may be pronounced with an internal glottal (fn.14).
new_statements.identity_note: Werner 1997 distinguishes two Ket tone systems, South Ket versus North (and Central) Ket, differing in the fourth tone and partly in the lexical distribution of tones; the open excerpt describes all dialects. The Jazyki mira tone table (on-disk file, not a listed work) is given for the Central Ket dialect. Georg 2007 (existing statement) is not dialect-labelled here.

The "sixth" contour is considerably rarer'; :60 'The default rule is that the first two syllables of the phonological word receive one of the two disyllabic contours.. most common is the fifth contour'; Nefedov 2015:15 (after Vajda 2004:13) 'rising/falling pitch resembling word-initial stress' as the general case with second-syllable peak only in 'a few disyllabic words'; Vajda 2009 (WOLD) 'characteristically have a rising falling tone on the first two moras'. This also explains (without endorsing) StressTyp2's 'initial' code. Also fill the empty quote/cite/loc/grade fields from the domain quotation/the domain locator (Georg 2007:58-60).

sources.quote: Werner 1997:179: "Stress in words is free: sabot 'belongings', assano '...', usdlgat '(little) birches'. In the stressed syllable dynamic characteristics prevail, except in the realization of two special disyllabic accentual types: in one of them a rise of the fundamental pitch of the voice is observed on the first (stressed) syllable, in the other on the last (stressed) syllable, with equal intensity on both syllables: qorqun 'cuckoo', plural qorqun."
